analysis|02-20|1946|Ο Μάξιμος γίνεται Οικουμενικός Πατριάρχης|Maximos becomes Ecumenical Patriarch|Ecumenical Patriarch Benjamin had died and the Patriarchate had to elect a successor, in a difficult period for the Orthodox leadership of Constantinople. In post-war Constantinople the Greek community was still numerically significant, and the choice of the new Patriarch was of great importance. The Ecumenical Patriarchate represented Orthodox leadership in the East, with a historic role that went beyond the limits of Constantinople. // Maximos, Metropolitan of Chalcedon, was elected by vote of the Holy and Sacred Synod and took up the office. The election was carried out in accordance with the regulations of the Patriarchate, which provide for the participation of senior clergy. The election by the Holy Synod reflected the collective procedure of the Patriarchate, with the aim of internal cohesion of the institution. The choice of the new Patriarch was regarded as important for the continuation of the Greek presence in the city. // His patriarchate lasted until 1948, when he resigned for reasons of health. It was the period in which the difficult era of the Patriarchate in modern Turkey was beginning, with a limited community and political restrictions. The resignation of 1948 highlighted the difficulties of the period, when the Greek community of the City faced a shrinking presence and political restrictions.

analysis|02-20|2015|Η συμφωνία του Eurogroup|The Eurogroup agreement|The new SYRIZA government had been elected in January 2015 with a promise to end austerity. Negotiations with the lenders were tense, while the rescue programme was about to expire and the country faced the risk of financial strangulation. The Eurogroup agreement was a critical turning point, because it decided the course of the programme and the financing options of the country. // The agreement of 20 February extended the programme for four months, on the condition that Greece would submit a list of reforms. The agreement was a compromise and left many questions open. The disagreement over the content of the reforms reflected the difference of views between the Greek government and its partners about the measures for growth. // The disagreements continued and led to the referendum of July 2015 and to a new agreement for a third memorandum, which showed the limits of the government's negotiating options. This development showed how closely the political decision in Athens is tied to the decisions of the European institutions and of the Eurogroup. The agreement opened a new period of negotiations, with emphasis on measures that would demonstrate the government's will to honour its commitments to its partners.

analysis|02-21|1913|Απελευθερώνονται τα Ιωάννινα|Ioannina is liberated|Ioannina had for centuries been the largest city of Epirus and the centre of Ottoman administration, with a significant intellectual and commercial tradition. The city was the key to control of the region, so its liberation was of great importance for the Greek army. Epirus had a historic role in Hellenism, and its freedom was linked with struggles and with a long tradition of resistance to Ottoman rule. // During the Balkan War the Greek army besieged the city and, after the battle of Bizani, the Ottoman commander Esat Pasha surrendered the city. The surrender came after the defeat of the Ottoman forces at the fortifications. The siege of the city was part of the wider operation of the Balkan War, which involved many forces in the area. // The Greek army entered Ioannina and the region was soon incorporated into Greece. For the people of Epirus it was a moment of celebration, and the liberation remains an official local festival. The liberation of Ioannina is a milestone in the modern history of Epirus and is part of the collective memory of the region through events and ceremonies. The memory of the liberation is honoured by the local community as a key point in the modern history of the city.

analysis|02-21|1915|Παραιτείται ο Βενιζέλος|Venizelos resigns|In the First World War Eleftherios Venizelos wanted Greece to help the Entente at the Dardanelles, with the prospect of territorial gains. This position was linked with the vision of national completion and with the ambition of the country to take part in arranging post-war Europe. The National Schism was a deep political rupture, combining different conceptions of foreign policy, the role of the king and the relationship of the state with the forces of the Entente. // King Constantine and his military associates regarded the operation as dangerous, because they feared for the country's security. The disagreement over strategy was deep and widespread. The foreign policy of the time directly affected the internal balance, and the different choices divided the elites and the public. // The disagreement led to the resignation of Venizelos, without the conflict ending: within a few months he returned to power and the clash with the king deepened. The National Schism divided Greek society for years and left deep marks on political life. The conflict left a long political legacy, which affected the parties and the electoral behaviour of the following decades.

analysis|02-21|1973|Η κατάληψη της Νομικής Σχολής Αθηνών|The occupation of the Athens Law School|The dictatorship of the colonels had been imposed in April 1967 and had abolished political freedoms, imposing censorship, arrests and exile. In the universities the regime tried to control student organisations and had imposed appointed student representations, while students who resisted were persecuted or conscripted in a punitive manner. By early 1973 discontent had grown, and part of the youth was ready to express its opposition openly. // Students occupied the building of the Law School in central Athens and demanded free student elections and an end to the use of conscription as a means of intimidation. The occupation was one of the first mass and public acts of resistance in the capital, and it lasted several days, with students from many faculties taking part. The regime responded with police and with measures against those taking part. // The mobilisation showed that the dictatorship had not succeeded in winning over the youth and prepared the ground for the events of November 1973 at the Polytechnic. Today it is regarded as one of the prelude to the uprising and shows how student resistance matured gradually, before the fall of the junta in 1974.

analysis|02-21|1988|Ο Γιώργος Βασιλείου εκλέγεται πρόεδρος|Giorgos Vasileiou is elected president|In early 1988 the outgoing president Spyros Kyprianou did not seek the office again, and the presidential contest became open. The Cyprus problem remained unresolved after the Turkish invasion of 1974, and the candidates differed in how they would handle negotiations and relations with the two communities. Glafkos Clerides, leader of the Democratic Rally, was the main opponent. // Giorgos Vasileiou, a businessman with international connections, stood as an independent candidate and was supported by AKEL and other forces. In the second round he prevailed by a narrow margin and became the third president of the Republic of Cyprus. His election showed that the political sphere of Cyprus could change through the unity of different parties around one candidate. // His presidency lasted until 1993, with contacts on the Cyprus problem and a turn of the country towards a more active international policy, since Cyprus had already begun efforts to approach the European Communities. In the following elections of 1993 he lost to Clerides, and Vasileiou remained known as the businessman who reached the leadership of the island.

analysis|02-22|1821|Ο Αλέξανδρος Υψηλάντης περνά τον Προύθο|Alexander Ypsilantis crosses the Prut|The Philiki Etaireia, a secret organisation founded in 1814 in Odessa, had for years been preparing the uprising of the Greeks. In 1820 Alexander Ypsilantis, an officer of the Russian army and scion of a Phanariot family, became its leader. Because the organisation wanted to create wider mobilisation, it chose the Danubian Principalities as the first field, where the Greek population was substantial and there were Greek rulers. // On 22 February 1821 by the old calendar, Ypsilantis crossed the river Prut and entered Moldavia, issuing a proclamation calling on the Greeks to rise. The operation rested on the hope that Russia would help, but Tsar Alexander I disavowed the movement. The Sacred Band and other forces fought, but were defeated at the battle of Dragatsani in June. // Despite the failure, Ypsilantis's move was the beginning of the Greek Revolution and drew Ottoman strength to the north, while a few weeks later the Peloponnese rose up. The uprising in the Principalities remains in history as the sacrifice of the first fighters.

analysis|02-23|532|Ο Ιουστινιανός διατάζει την οικοδόμηση της Αγίας Σοφίας|Justinian orders the construction of Hagia Sophia|In January 532 Constantinople was shaken by the Nika riot, an uprising of the factions of the Hippodrome that almost overthrew Justinian I. The emperor managed to suppress it with the help of the generals Belisarius and Mundus, but the city had suffered great destruction, and the earlier church of Hagia Sophia had burned. // A few weeks later Justinian began the ambitious work of rebuilding, and the foundation was laid on 23 February 532. The architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, scientists with knowledge of mathematics and engineering. The work proceeded at an impressive speed and was completed in less than six years, in 537. // The church with its enormous dome became the largest and tallest building in Christendom for centuries, and a symbol of the power and piety of the empire. It later served as a church, as a mosque, and today as a monument, and it remains one of the most important achievements of world architecture.

analysis|02-23|1943|Η πολιτική επιστράτευση στην Κατοχή|Political conscription during the Occupation|During the Occupation the Germans needed labour for their industry, since the war machine had caused shortages of personnel. The occupation government of Konstantinos Logothetopoulos, and later of Ioannis Rallis, was under German pressure and accepted the demand to send Greek workers to Germany. The population had already suffered from the great famine of 1941-1942. // In February 1943 the political conscription of certain age groups was announced. The news provoked a nationwide reaction, with the participation of EAM and other organisations. In Athens large demonstrations took place, with students and workers coming out onto the streets, and clashes with the authorities occurred, with casualties. // The government was forced to suspend the measure, and in effect it succeeded in preventing the Germans from sending Greeks to Germany on a mass scale. The victory is regarded as one of the most important moments of the Resistance, because it showed the power of popular mobilisation even under the rule of the occupier.

analysis|02-23|1969|Πεθαίνει ο στρατηγός Ρόναλντ Σκόμπι|General Ronald Scobie dies|Ronald Scobie was a British officer who commanded the British forces in Greece in the autumn of 1944, when the Germans withdrew. The British forces had been sent to support the national unity government of Georgios Papandreou and to secure the handing over of weapons by the resistance organisations. // In the Dekemvriana of 1944 the clash between ELAS and the government and British forces in Athens became the first major round of the civil rivalry. Scobie had a role in the operations and in shaping British policy, and he imposed measures against ELAS, which made him a controversial figure. // The historical judgement of his role is divided. For some he was the soldier who protected the government and prevented the KKE from seizing power; for others he was the representative of a foreign intervention that deepened the divisions. He died in London in 1969, and his name remains bound up with the Dekemvriana.

analysis|02-24|1975|Αποκαλύπτεται απόπειρα πραξικοπήματος|A coup attempt is uncovered|After the fall of the dictatorship in the summer of 1974, the country began the Metapolitefsi under the government of Konstantinos Karamanlis. The new regime had to consolidate democracy, while the army still contained officers who had links with the junta and resented the changes. In addition, the Turkish invasion of Cyprus had caused tension. // On 24 February 1975 the Minister of National Defence, Evangelos Averoff, announced that a plan for a coup by military men had been uncovered, and that those involved had been arrested before they could act. The disclosure showed that democracy was still fragile. // The government brought the situation under control, and the trial of those arrested followed. The event strengthened the position of those who demanded a stricter restructuring of the armed forces and the punishment of the protagonists of the junta. A few months later, in the summer of 1975, the trials of the principal perpetrators of the dictatorship took place, and democracy was consolidated.

analysis|02-24|1981|Ο σεισμός των Αλκυονίδων|The Alkyonides earthquake|The Gulf of Corinth is an area of intense seismic activity, because it lies on a fault along which the Earth is continually stretched. On 24 February 1981 a strong earthquake of 6.7 on the Richter scale struck the area, with its epicentre in the Gulf of Alkyonides. A few days later two more large earthquakes followed, which worsened the situation. // The earthquake caused great damage in Corinth, where many houses became unfit for habitation, and in parts of Attica and Central Greece. Several buildings in Athens suffered damage, and there were victims and injured. Thousands of people were left homeless and had to be housed temporarily. // The event highlighted the need for anti-seismic planning and safer construction, and it was one of the largest earthquakes of post-war Greece. It contributed to the strengthening of regulations and to the creation of civil protection mechanisms for dealing with natural disasters.

analysis|02-24|1994|Η Βουλή αναγνωρίζει τη Γενοκτονία των Ποντίων|Parliament recognises the Pontian Genocide|The Greeks of Pontus, on the south-eastern coast of the Black Sea, suffered persecution, deportations and massacres in the period 1914-1923, at the end of the Ottoman Empire and in the early years of the new Turkish national movement. The survivors came to Greece as refugees, especially after the population exchange and the Asia Minor Catastrophe. // For decades the memory was kept alive in the families and associations of the Pontians. In 1994 the Greek Parliament unanimously passed a resolution recognising the events as genocide and designating 19 May, the day that symbolises the start of Mustafa Kemal's movement in Amisos, as a day of remembrance. // The resolution gave official recognition to the collective traumatic experience of the Pontians and became a field for commemorative events and educational activities. Turkey rejects the characterisation, and the question continues to occupy historical debate and international relations.

analysis|02-24|2008|Ο Δημήτρης Χριστόφιας εκλέγεται πρόεδρος|Dimitris Christofias is elected president|In early 2008 Cyprus had already joined the European Union and the euro was on the threshold, while the Cyprus problem remained unresolved after the rejection of the Annan Plan in 2004. The outgoing president Tassos Papadopoulos, who had been judged harsh in his politics, was eliminated from the second round. // Dimitris Christofias, general secretary of AKEL, defeated Ioannis Kasoulides in the second round and became president. He was the first communist leader of a member state of the EU, and this made his election an international news item. He expressed the expectation of resuming talks with the Turkish Cypriot leader. // His presidency lasted until 2013 and was marked by negotiations with Mehmet Ali Talat and later with Dervis Eroglu, by the explosion at the naval base Evangelos Florakis in 2011, and by the economic crisis that led to a request for support from partners.

analysis|02-24|2013|Ο Νίκος Αναστασιάδης εκλέγεται πρόεδρος|Nikos Anastasiades is elected president|In early 2013 Cyprus was in a deep economic crisis: the banks had suffered considerable losses, especially from their exposure to Greek bonds, and the government of Dimitris Christofias was seeking support from partners. The election was regarded as critical, since the new president would have to negotiate the rescue programme. // Nikos Anastasiades, leader of the Democratic Rally, defeated Stavros Malas, candidate of AKEL, in the second round. Within a few weeks of taking office the country was at the centre of international attention, as the Eurogroup of March 2013 agreed measures that included a haircut on deposits in banks and restrictions on capital movements. // The election brought a period of intense economic adjustment and, later, recovery. Anastasiades was re-elected in 2018 and was president until 2023, and in the Cyprus problem he took part in negotiations such as the Crans-Montana conference of 2017.

analysis|02-25|1822|Καταργείται η δουλεία στην Ελλάδα|Slavery is abolished in Greece|In the first year of the Revolution the fighters fought on many fronts and had to organise politically. The First National Assembly of Epidaurus, which convened in early 1822, voted the Provisional Constitution of Greece, which proclaimed basic rights and laid the foundations of the newly formed state. // In this spirit the revolutionary administration established freedom for those held in slavery in the territories of the Revolution, and the measure was included among the basic principles of the new political order. The period is characterised by the influence of the ideas of the Enlightenment and the French Revolution, which affected Greek scholars. // The regulation showed that the struggle was not only a war for independence from the Ottomans, but also an attempt towards a society with liberties and equality before the law. Its application in a country at war was difficult, but the symbol remains strong in the history of Greek institutions.

analysis|02-25|1968|Ο Μακάριος επανεκλέγεται πρόεδρος|Makarios is re-elected president|Makarios III, archbishop and first president of the Republic of Cyprus since 1960, had found himself at the centre of intense upheavals on the island. After the intercommunal clashes of 1963-1964 and the crisis of 1967 with the dictatorial Greece, Cyprus faced deep political uncertainty. The elections of 1968 were called to renew his mandate. // Makarios was elected by an overwhelming majority and with very high voter turnout, which strengthened his position against his political opponents and in Athens. The election was regarded as a popular mandate for the continuation of his policy, with strong independence for the island. // The confirmation of popular support did not solve the problems. In the following years the relations of Makarios with the junta and with extremist organisations worsened, culminating in the coup of July 1974 and the Turkish invasion. The election of 1968 reflects his strong position as ethnarch of Cyprus at that time.

analysis|02-25|1973|Η κατάληψη της Νομικής Σχολής|The occupation of the Law School|In early 1973 the dictatorship of the colonels had completed almost six years, with limited social support and growing criticism. Students, who faced control of student associations and the threat of conscription for those who protested, had begun to organise secretly and issue leaflets. // On that day thousands of students fortified themselves in the building of the Law School on Solonos Street and demanded democratic freedoms. The occupation made a great impression, because it took place in the centre of the city and was supported by other citizens too. The police eventually intervened and arrests followed. // The events showed that resistance was becoming mass and more open. About nine months later, in November 1973, the uprising of the Polytechnic would shake the regime, and this is regarded as the climax of the student mobilisation. The occupation of the Law School remains an important milestone on the road to the fall of the dictatorship.

analysis|02-26|1822|Λεηλασία της Χαλανδρίτσας|The plunder of Chalandritsa|In Achaea the Revolution had broken out in the spring of 1821 and the Greeks had captured positions in the countryside, while Patras and its castle remained under Ottoman control. Chalandritsa was an important small town and seat of the revolutionaries in the area, and its destruction would have had both military and psychological significance. // Ottoman forces, about two thousand men, moved against it and destroyed it, burned houses and plundered possessions. The inhabitants fled to the surrounding mountains, and many lost their belongings. Such attacks showed the cruelty of the war, which also struck civilians. // The destruction did not put an end to the struggle in Achaea, where the Greeks continued operations with the help of local chieftains. It is one of the episodes that recall the heavy price paid by the civilian population in the early years of the Revolution.

analysis|02-26|2020|Το πρώτο κρούσμα κορονοϊού στην Ελλάδα|The first coronavirus case in Greece|In early 2020 the new coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 had appeared in China and spread quickly across Europe, with Italy becoming the first major European centre. The Greek government followed developments and had prepared a plan of response, while hospitals were told to be on alert. // On 26 February the first case of COVID-19 in the country was confirmed, in a woman from Thessaloniki who had travelled to Italy. In the following weeks the number of cases rose, and the government took measures such as closing schools and, at the end of March, a general restriction of movement. // Greece faced the first wave with a relatively small number of deaths compared with other countries, which was attributed to the timely measures. However, the pandemic deeply affected the economy, especially tourism, and daily life, and it left its mark as one of the most important crises of the modern era.

analysis|02-27|380|Το Διάταγμα της Θεσσαλονίκης|The Edict of Thessalonica|Christianity had been legalised by Constantine in 313, but for decades there were intense disputes, especially between the followers of the Nicene faith and the Arians. Theodosius I, who had ascended the throne of the East in 379, was in Thessalonica, where he fell seriously ill and was baptised. // On 27 February 380 he issued, together with his co-emperors Gratian and Valentinian II, an edict that required the peoples of the empire to follow the faith taught by the bishop of Rome and the bishop of Alexandria, that is, the Nicene Christian faith. The text was addressed to the inhabitants of Constantinople, but it had a more general significance. // The edict is regarded as a milestone, because it made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the state and subjected to sanctions those who disagreed. In 381 the Second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople confirmed the doctrine, and in the following years the old cults were gradually restricted. The decision defined the relationship between state and Church in Byzantium.

analysis|02-27|425|Ο Θεοδόσιος Β΄ ιδρύει το Πανδιδακτήριο|Theodosius II founds the Pandidakterion|Constantinople had become a great capital, with an administration that needed educated officials, lawyers and orators. Educational activity had already existed in the city, with private teachers, but an organised state institution of higher education was lacking. Theodosius II was known for his interest in letters and in legislation. // In 425, at the urging of his wife Athenais-Eudocia, who was educated and came from Athens, he founded the Pandidakterion. The decree provided chairs for teachers of grammar, rhetoric, philosophy and law, for both Greek and Latin. // The institution is regarded as a forerunner of the university and one of the oldest state educational establishments, and it contributed to the preservation of classical education. Its functions were reorganised many times later, but its foundation showed the importance that Byzantium gave to knowledge and to the training of the state apparatus.

analysis|02-27|1869|Εγκαινιάζεται ο σιδηρόδρομος Αθήνας–Πειραιά|The Athens–Piraeus railway is inaugurated|In the mid-19th century the connection of Athens with the port of Piraeus was made by road and cart, and the growth of trade made a better transport system urgent. Greece was still in the early stages of industrialisation, and the railway was regarded as a symbol of modernisation. // The line, about nine kilometres long, was inaugurated in 1869 and became the first railway connection in the country. It linked Thiseio with Piraeus and allowed the rapid transport of passengers and goods. The project was carried out by a private company with foreign capital. // The line was strengthened with the development of Athens and Piraeus, and over time was electrified and integrated into the present-day electric railway. It remains one of the oldest useful transport lines of the capital and forms part of the history of public transport in Greece.

analysis|02-27|1938|Γεννιέται ο Ευαγόρας Παλληκαρίδης|Evagoras Pallikarides is born|Evagoras Pallikarides was born in Lysi, Cyprus, at a time when the island was a British colony. Greek Cypriots demanded union with Greece, and this demand fuelled the EOKA struggle that began in 1955. Pallikarides grew up in this climate and studied at the Pancyprian Gymnasium in Nicosia. // As a pupil he became involved in demonstrations and joined EOKA, taking part in the organisation's actions. He was arrested by the British authorities and sentenced to death for illegal possession of weapons and participation in attacks. // On 14 March 1957 he was hanged in the Central Prison of Nicosia, at a very young age. His attitude before the execution and the letter he left made him a symbol of courage and self-sacrifice for Cypriots. He is honoured every year, and many schools and streets in Cyprus and Greece bear his name.

analysis|02-27|1968|Ο Ανδρέας Παπανδρέου ανακοινώνει την ίδρυση του ΠΑΚ|Andreas Papandreou announces the founding of PAK|After the coup of 21 April 1967, Andreas Papandreou, who was an MP of the Centre Union and son of Georgios Papandreou, was arrested and after his release left for abroad. He sought to organise an international movement of resistance to the dictatorship and to inform international public opinion. // In Stockholm in 1968 he announced the founding of the Panhellenic Liberation Movement (PAK), an organisation that demanded the overthrow of the junta and operated abroad with events, publications and contacts with politicians. Members of the movement also took part in actions against the regime. // PAK did not bring about the overthrow of the dictatorship, but it increased international pressure and established Andreas Papandreou as a leading figure of the anti-junta opposition. After 1974 he founded PASOK, which took power in 1981.

analysis|02-27|1991|Η Αλέκα Παπαρήγα επικεφαλής του ΚΚΕ|Aleka Paparega heads the KKE|The KKE was passing through a critical period at the beginning of the 1990s. The collapse of the regimes of Eastern Europe and the split of the party in 1991, when part of its cadres followed the Coalition of the Left, created a deep political crisis. The historic leader Charilaos Florakis left the general secretariat. // At the 13th Congress of the party Aleka Paparega was elected general secretary. She was the first woman to lead a Greek party with a parliamentary presence, which was significant in a political life with limited female representation. // Under her leadership the KKE kept its identity and its disagreement with the European Union, with a steady electoral strength. She remained general secretary until 2013. Her election became a historic moment in Greek politics.

analysis|02-28|1914|Η αυτονομία της Βορείου Ηπείρου|Northern Epirus is granted autonomy|Northern Epirus, with a considerable Greek population, was an area that after the Balkan Wars was disputed between Greece and Albania. The Protocol of Florence, at the end of 1913, assigned the region to the newly created Albania, and the Greek army withdrew from the area. // The Greek residents proclaimed the Autonomous State of Northern Epirus at Argyrokastro, with Georgios Christakis-Zografos as president and experienced officials from Greece. The proclamation was made on 28 February 1914 by the new calendar, and local forces confronted the Albanian forces. // With the Protocol of Corfu, in May 1914, Northern Epirus received a special status of autonomy within Albania. The First World War overturned the system, and the question returned later. The question of the rights of the Greek minority remains open in Greek-Albanian relations.

analysis|02-28|1943|Η κηδεία του Παλαμά|The funeral of Palamas|Kostis Palamas, the National Poet, died in Athens on 27 February 1943, at the age of 83. The country was living under the Occupation, with famine, strict restrictions and danger for those who demonstrated publicly. Even so, the news of his death moved the public, who saw in the poet a symbol of national consciousness. // The funeral took place in the First Cemetery of Athens and a large crowd followed it, in an effective act of resistance. Angelos Sikelianos recited his poem "Let the Trumpets Sound", and those present sang the National Anthem, despite the presence of the conquerors. // The funeral is regarded as one of the most moving events of the Occupation, because it showed that intellectual life and national feeling had not been suppressed. Palamas remains in history as the poet of "The Twelve Words of the Gypsy" and of the "Hymn" for the first Olympic Games of 1896.

analysis|02-28|2023|Το σιδηροδρομικό δυστύχημα στα Τέμπη|The Tempi railway disaster|The Greek railway network had for years faced problems of understaffing, poor maintenance and delayed modernisation of its safety and remote control systems. The Athens–Thessaloniki line is the main axis of the network and served large numbers of passengers and freight. On the evening of 28 February 2023, during a holiday period with many students on the trains, traffic was heavier than usual. // In the area of Tempi, near Larissa, a passenger train collided head-on with a freight train. The collision caused a fire and the destruction of the first carriages, and 57 people were lost, many of them young. The rescue and identification of the victims lasted many days. // The disaster provoked deep anger and large demonstrations across the country, with demands for accountability and safety in transport. The Minister of Transport resigned, and investigations and judicial proceedings followed. The case opened a debate about the condition of the infrastructure and the accountability of the state, and it continues to occupy political and social life.

analysis|02-29|1944|Η Συμφωνία της Πλάκας|The Plaka Agreement|From 1943 the largest resistance organisations, ELAS of EAM and EDES of Napoleon Zervas, had been fighting each other in Epirus, although the common enemy was the occupying forces. These clashes weakened the Resistance and worried the Allies, especially Britain, which had sent missions to the mountains. // Through the mediation of the British mission, an agreement was signed at Plaka in Epirus between EAM-ELAS, EDES and EKKA, by which hostilities ceased and the organisations committed themselves to turn against the conquerors. It also provided for the definition of zones of action. // The agreement temporarily reduced the clashes, but did not solve the deeper political problem, namely the dispute over the post-war political regime of the country. Mistrust continued, and a few months later, after the liberation, the Dekemvriana broke out and later the Civil War.

analysis|03-01|1923|Η Ελλάδα περνά στο Γρηγοριανό ημερολόγιο|Greece switches to the Gregorian calendar|Until 1923 Greece used the Julian calendar, which was thirteen days behind the Gregorian, which had been adopted in Western Europe from the 16th century and later in most countries. This created problems in transactions, diplomacy and trade. The change had been discussed earlier. // In 1923 the government decided on the change: 16 February by the old calendar became 1 March. The Church of Greece accepted the new calendar for fixed feasts, while Easter and the movable feasts continued to be calculated in the traditional way. // The change was also a cause of disagreement. Part of the faithful reacted, and the Old Calendarists were formed, who still follow the Julian calendar. For the record, this date explains why many events before 1923 have two dates and why it must be stated which calendar they are recorded in.

analysis|03-01|1935|Το βενιζελικό κίνημα του 1935|The Venizelist movement of 1935|After the defeat of the Liberals in the elections of 1933 and the assassination attempt on Venizelos, political life was marked by a sharp division between Venizelists and anti-Venizelists. A large number of army and navy officers, friendly to Venizelos, were concerned about purges and about the turn of the government of Panagis Tsaldaris towards the monarchy. // On 1 March 1935 the officers launched a movement, centred on the navy and with bases in Macedonia and Crete. Venizelos was in Crete and placed himself at the side of the insurgents. The government forces, led by General Georgios Kondylis, suppressed the movement within a few days. // Trials and executions followed, purges in the armed forces and the flight of Venizelos, who died in Paris in 1936. The failure gave the anti-Venizelists the opportunity to abolish the republican system and restore the monarchy in autumn 1935, paving the way to the dictatorship of Metaxas.

analysis|03-01|1959|Ο Μακάριος επιστρέφει στην Κύπρο|Makarios returns to Cyprus|Archbishop Makarios III had been arrested by the British in 1956 and exiled to the Seychelles. He was released in 1957, but was not allowed to return to Cyprus and lived in Athens.
